name: bluewater-09-first-screen
lines: At seven forty this morning, somebody landed on your website.
By seven forty one, she was gone.
She didn't call. She didn't fill in the form. She hit the back button and called the next name.
And here's the part that should bother you. You already paid to get her there.
So let's talk about that one minute. Because it's probably happening to you right now.
Let me show you with a guy I invented. His name is Theo, and he fixes garage doors.
Fourteen years. He can hear a bad spring from the driveway. If your door is stuck, he's the one you want.
And this is Nadia. It's seven forty. Her garage door won't open, and her car is inside.
She has a meeting at eight thirty. So she grabs her phone and searches garage door repair.
Theo's name comes up. She taps it. Good. That was the hard part.
Now watch what she sees.
A photo of a house that isn't from anywhere near here. A menu with nine things in it.
Welcome to our website. We pride ourselves on quality and service since 2011.
She scrolls. About us. Our mission. A paragraph about springs.
Where's the phone number? It's at the very bottom. In grey.
She never gets that far. Back button.
The next site says, garage door stuck? We come today. Tap to call.
She taps. That's Hank. Hank has been doing this for two years.
Hank gets the job. Three hundred and forty dollars. And Theo never knew she was there.
Now do the math with me. Say that happens to Theo three times a week.
Three jobs, at three forty, fifty weeks a year. That's fifty one thousand dollars.
Not lost to a better company. Lost to a better first screen.
That night, Theo finally looks at his own website. On his phone. The way a customer does.
He's never done that. He built it on a computer six years ago and never opened it again.
He can't find his own phone number.
Here's the truth about your website. Nobody reads it. They glance at it.
A customer with a problem gives you a few seconds to answer three questions.
Do you fix my problem? Do you come to my area? How do I reach you right now?
If your first screen answers those three, you get the call. If it doesn't, nothing else on the site matters.
So here are three fixes. You can check every one of them tonight, on your phone.
Fix one. The first screen.
Before anyone scrolls, they should see three things.
What you do, in plain words. Garage door repair.
Where you do it. Burnaby and New West.
And a button that calls you. Big. At the top. One tap.
Theo deletes welcome to our website. Nobody has ever needed to be welcomed.
He writes this instead. Garage door stuck? We fix it today, in Burnaby and New West.
That one sentence does more work than the whole old page.
Fix two. Show them it's really you.
That stock photo of a perfect house? Your customer has seen it on four other sites this morning.
Use your own. Your truck. Your face. A door you fixed last week.
A real photo that's a little crooked beats a perfect one that could be anybody.
Then put your reviews right there on the page. Not on another tab. Right under the button.
Now she knows three things in five seconds. You do it. You're close. And other people trust you.
Fix three. Make the next step tiny.
Theo's contact form had nine boxes. Address. Postal code. Door model. How did you hear about us.
She's standing in a cold garage with one free thumb. She is not typing a postal code.
Three boxes. Name. Phone. What's wrong.
And pin the call button to the bottom of the screen, so wherever she scrolls, it follows her thumb.
One more. Answer the question everybody has. What's this going to cost me?
You don't need an exact price. Give a range. Most repairs run between this and that.
If people can't tell whether they can afford you, a lot of them won't call to ask. They'll just leave.
Now, Hank. Hank hears that websites matter, so he pays for a fancy one. Video background. Sliding pictures. Music.
It takes eleven seconds to load on a phone. And the call button is hiding under an animation.
A website isn't there to impress anybody. It's there to make the phone ring.
Three weeks later. Seven forty in the morning. A different garage. A different car stuck inside.
Same search. Same tap. Theo's site opens.
Garage door stuck? We fix it today. His truck. His face. Forty one reviews. A big blue button.
She doesn't scroll. She doesn't read. She taps.
Theo's phone rings while he's loading the truck.
Three hundred and forty dollars. To the right guy this time. It took her four seconds.
I can't promise you a website wins every job. Nobody can.
But when a site loses a customer, it's rarely the design. It's the first screen.
Theo didn't rebuild anything. Same site. Same address. He changed one screen, three photos and a form.
Two things to stay away from.
Don't start over from scratch because someone said it looks dated. Fix the first screen first.
And don't test it on your computer. Your customers aren't on one. Test it on a phone, with one thumb.
So here's your test. It takes five minutes, and you need one other person.
Open your site on your phone. Hand it to someone who's never seen it. Count to five. Take it back.
Then ask three questions. What do we do? Where do we do it? How would you reach us?
If they can't answer all three, you just found out what happened at seven forty one.
Theo's number was fifty one thousand dollars. Yours will be different. But it isn't zero.
First screen. Real photos. Tiny next step.
And if you'd rather have someone go through your site with you, that's exactly the kind of thing we do at Bluewater.
